extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical criteria for making and evaluating aesthetic judgements of beauty and the sublime, focusing on conditions (universality, disinterestedness), the role of imagination/understanding, and the distinction between beautiful and sublime (mathematical vs dynamic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition of necessity for judgement of taste: Idea of a common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition of necessity which a judgement of taste asserts is the Idea of a common sense; judgements of taste must rest on a subjective principle (feeling, not concepts) but yet claim universal validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes 'common sense' (result of free play of cognitive powers) from common understanding (sensus communis). The claim of necessity depends on presupposing a common sense as the ground of anticipating universal assent, provided particulars are correctly subsumed under that ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal communicability of cognitions and feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitions and judgements, along with the conviction that accompanies them, must admit of universal communicability; feelings accompanying representations must likewise be communicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This communicability is the subjective condition of cognition and is presupposed as necessary for knowledge (and thus for judgments of taste). It is not derived from psychological observation but posited as necessary for universal communicability in logic and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste claims an 'ought' (subjective necessity represented as objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one declares something beautiful one attributes not merely that others will agree but that they ought to agree; the principle concerning agreement of judging persons is subjective yet assumed as subjectively universal (an Idea necessary for everyone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ideal norm (common sense) gives judgements of taste an exemplary validity: a right to make one's judgement a rule for everyone, contingent on correct subsumption of particulars under the norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful is that which without any concept is cognised as the object of a necessary satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty is experienced without reference to determinate concepts; the satisfaction is represented as necessary (claims universal validity) even though grounded only in feeling, not conceptual cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as faculty referencing imagination's free conformity to law (purposiveness without purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty for judging an object in reference to the Imagination’s free conformity to law: the Imagination should be free and yet of itself conform to law—'purposiveness without purpose'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Imagination is conceived as productive/spontaneous (not merely reproductive). The free play of Imagination and Understanding (mutual accord) is central; this free conformity is distinct from conformity determined by concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity/disinterestedness of judgement of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure judgement of taste combines satisfaction or dissatisfaction without any reference to use or purpose — it is disinterested (devoid of interest in the object's existence or practical use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Imagination's product is determined by concepts (aimed at cognition or use), the satisfaction pertains to the Good (perfection) not the Beautiful. Pure taste must avoid teleological or utilitarian considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity tied to concept is not pure beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrically regular figures (circle, square, cube) are regular because we represent them under definite concepts; such regularity yields satisfaction tied to cognition, not to pure taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where form is grasped by a definite concept (useful for design, measurement), the pleasure is cognitive/practical rather than the disinterested pleasure of pure taste. Critics who call such regularity 'indisputable beauty' conflate cognitive approval with aesthetic taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of rigid mathematical regularity for pure taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Stiff or mathematical regularity tends to repel taste because it imposes constraint and produces weariness rather than sustained aesthetic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contexts where free play of Imagination is valued (e.g., pleasure gardens, furniture), freedom from constraint and novelty sustain taste. Excessive regularity entertains only briefly and is not suited to aesthetic contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained interest from free, purposive play and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects that allow the Imagination to play freely in a purposive, unstudied manner are always new to us and do not tire the observer, thereby better satisfying taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: wild natural variety, freedom near the grotesque in garden or furniture design. Contrast with repeated, rule-bound music or architecture which we weary of sooner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between beautiful objects and beautiful views
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful objects (recognizable with form) differ from beautiful views of objects (distant or unclear) where taste appears more in the imaginative fancies aroused than in clear apprehension of form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing forms (fire, rippling brook) may not be 'beautiful' in a strict sense but charm the Imagination by stimulating free play and fiction-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime as representation of boundlessness with totality present to thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime is found in that which, though formless, represents boundlessness while its totality is present to thought; it is associated with quantity rather than the quality emphasized in the Beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublime experiences refer to Ideas of Reason; sensible forms cannot fully contain the sublime proper. The sublime is an effect in the mind (attitude of thought) rather than a property residing fully in natural form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective character of the Sublime: negative pleasure (admiration/respect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure of the Sublime is indirect and often negative — a feeling of admiration or respect produced by a momentary checking of the vital powers and a consequent stronger outflow of them; it is earnest rather than playful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike the Beautiful (which furthers life and invites playful contemplation), the Sublime alternately attracts and repels, producing a kind of respect rather than charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime is located in ideas of Reason, not in nature's purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime concerns Ideas of Reason (supersensible ideas) that cannot be adequately presented sensibly; nature may occasion the feeling but does not itself contain purposive forms corresponding to the Sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural phenomena (e.g., stormy ocean) may appear horrible rather than sublime unless the mind is already filled with manifold Ideas enabling a turn from sensibility to Reason. Thus the source is internal (our use of representation), not objective purposiveness in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic division for judging the Sublime: quantity, quality, relation, modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetical judgments about the Sublime should be represented according to quantity (universal validity), quality (devoid of interest), relation (subjective purposiveness), and modality (necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method mirrors the analysis of judgements of taste, but begins with quantity because the Sublime often concerns formlessness/size rather than form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold Sublime: mathematically and dynamically sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime divides into the mathematically sublime (related to magnitude) and the dynamically sublime (related to might/power), reflecting whether the Imagination's movement is referred to cognition or desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical Sublime arises from immensity that challenges comprehension; Dynamic Sublime arises from ideas of overwhelming power (threat) judged against our moral or rational standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematically Sublime: 'absolutely great' beyond comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematically Sublime is that which is 'absolutely great' — great beyond all comparison — and thus cannot be adequately measured by any sensible standard; it is a magnitude that shows itself like no other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because all sensible magnitudes are comparable, nothing in sense alone is truly sublime; the feeling arises from the inadequacy of our faculty for estimating magnitude and the Idea of the infinite in Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic estimation of magnitude: apprehension vs comprehensio aesthetica
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimation of magnitude in intuition involves apprehension (which can proceed indefinitely) and comprehension (comprehensio aesthetica), which has a maximum; the Sublime emerges when comprehension is strained or inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: viewing the Pyramids or St. Peter's — full emotional effect requires distance neither too near nor too far. Mathematical (numerical) estimation differs from aesthetic, which relies on a subjective maximal comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for a pure judgement of the Sublime (disinterested, not teleological, prefer 'rude' nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure judgement of the Sublime must be disinterested (no practical purpose or teleological judgement) and should not be exhibited in products of art or in natural objects whose concepts carry definite purposes; best found in rude nature merely containing magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mixing teleological judgements (purposeful design) with the aesthetic judgement of the sublime. Monstrous objects (destroying the concept's purpose by size) or artful constructions are not suitable for pure aesthetic Sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime as sign of supersensible faculty: ability to think the infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: The experience of the Sublime signals the mind's capacity to think the infinite (a faculty surpassing every standard of sense), i.e., the reflective judgement's recognition of Reason's Ideas beyond sensible representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is the state of mind produced by certain representations — the capacity to think totality or the infinite without contradiction — that marks the Sublime, not any mere sensible object.
